gifToSprite.tipsTitle: Did You Know? GIF to Spritesheet Tips
tips: Use the **Padding** option to add pixel gaps between frames in your sprite sheet. This prevents texture bleeding — a common rendering artifact in game engines where adjacent frames leak into each other.
Enable **Remove Background** to automatically detect and remove solid-color backgrounds from each frame. The algorithm samples the four corner pixels to find the background color.

The hex color picker includes an **eyedropper tool** — click it to pick any color directly from the preview image or anywhere on your screen. This is perfect for selecting the exact background color when auto-detection doesn't match.
Adjust the **Tolerance** slider to control how aggressively similar colors are removed. A value of 30 works for most clean backgrounds, while 50–80 handles gradients or compression artifacts.

toGif.tipsTitle: Did You Know? PNG to GIF Tips
tips: Set **Frame Duration** to control animation speed. 100ms gives a smooth 10 FPS animation, while 50ms creates a fast 20 FPS effect. Most pixel art animations look best at 80–120ms.
Enable **Sort by Filename** when your frames use a naming convention like walk_0.png, walk_1.png. The tool will sort by the numeric suffix instead of upload order.
If your frames have **different sizes**, choose "Center on transparent canvas" to automatically align them on the largest frame's dimensions without cropping.
In **Spritesheet mode**, use the grid preview overlay to verify your column and row settings before converting. The red lines show exactly where the tool will slice.

Use **Trim Margins** to crop extra borders around your spritesheet before slicing. Many exported spritesheets have outer padding that isn't part of the frame grid — trimming it ensures accurate cell alignment.

pngToSpritesheet.tipsTitle: Did You Know? PNG to Spritesheet Tips
tips: Drag frames in the upload grid to reorder them — the order you see is the frame order in the final atlas.
Use the **Packed layout** for mixed-size assets like UI icons — bin-packing fits irregular shapes ~2× more efficiently than a fixed grid.
Enable **JSON Metadata** to export a TexturePacker-compatible JSON file — load it directly in Phaser 3 with `scene.load.atlas()` or in PixiJS with `Assets.load()`.
Enable **Power of 2** if your engine requires GPU-friendly texture dimensions — required for WebGL 1 `GL_REPEAT` samplers and older mobile GPUs.
Have frames with transparent borders? Try our **PNG Trim** tool first — cropping empty edges before packing produces a tighter, more efficient atlas.

pngTrim.tipsTitle: Did You Know? PNG Trim Tips
tips: The **Alpha Threshold** controls which pixels count as transparent — 0 removes only fully empty pixels, while higher values (e.g., 10–30) also trim semi-transparent halos and anti-aliasing fringes.
Add a **Padding** value to keep a thin transparent margin around each sprite — a 1–2px buffer prevents texture bleeding when adjacent sprites share a cell in a game engine atlas.
Upload multiple PNG files at once — all trimmed files are returned in a single ZIP archive with original filenames preserved, ready to drop into your project.
After trimming, use our **PNG to Spritesheet** tool to pack all cleaned frames into a single texture atlas — ready for Phaser 3, PixiJS, Unity, or Godot in one step.

splitSpritesheet.tipsTitle: Did You Know? Spritesheet Splitter Tips
tips: Use **Column Range** and **Row Range** to extract only a specific animation from a multi-sequence sheet — for example, Row Range "2-3" pulls just rows 2 and 3 without extracting the whole atlas.
**Skip Empty** is on by default and automatically discards fully transparent cells — turn it off only if your animation deliberately uses blank frames (e.g., a pause in a blink cycle).
**JSON Array metadata** is natively understood by Phaser 3 (`scene.load.atlas`) and PixiJS (`Assets.load`) with no extra setup — load the ZIP contents and every frame is addressable by name.
Set **Cell Padding** to match the gap between frames in your source spritesheet — many TexturePacker or Aseprite exports include 1–2px gutters that must be accounted for before slicing.
Need to clean up the extracted frames? Run them through our **PNG Trim** tool to crop transparent edges, then re-pack into a new spritesheet with **PNG to Spritesheet**.

heicToJpg.tipsTitle: Did You Know? HEIC to JPG Tips
tips: **HEIC** is Apple's default iPhone photo format — great compression but poorly supported outside the Apple ecosystem. JPG works everywhere from Windows to webmail to print labs.
Use **Quality 85–92** for photos: you'll rarely see a visible difference vs the original, and file size drops by 30–50% compared to quality 100.
The tool strips EXIF orientation and rewrites pixels in their correct rotation, so photos no longer appear sideways in apps that don't read EXIF.
Batch uploading via the API? The same engine powers our RapidAPI endpoint — send a multipart POST and stream JPGs back, no user interaction needed.

heicToPng.tipsTitle: Did You Know? HEIC to PNG Tips
tips: Use **HEIC → PNG** when you need **lossless** quality — no compression artifacts, perfect pixel fidelity. Ideal for photo editing workflows where you'll re-encode later.
PNG preserves the full **alpha channel** from HEIC if your source supports it (iPhone Portrait Mode depth masks, for example).
PNG files are typically 3–5× larger than HEIC. Convert only when the extra size is acceptable — for web use, prefer WebP or JPG.
After converting to PNG, you can use our **PNG Trim** tool to crop transparent edges, or **PNG to WebP** to shrink them back down for web delivery.

heicToWebp.tipsTitle: Did You Know? HEIC to WebP Tips
tips: WebP compresses ~25–35% better than JPG at the same visual quality, and it supports transparency — the best all-round choice for modern web photos.
Use **Lossless mode** sparingly: WebP lossless is 2–5× larger than lossy and rarely necessary for photos. Reserve it for screenshots or UI graphics.
All modern browsers (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari 14+) support WebP natively. For iOS < 14 fallback, convert to JPG instead.
WebP is Google's preferred format for Core Web Vitals — using it can directly improve your Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) scores.

pngToJpg.tipsTitle: Did You Know? PNG to JPG Tips
tips: PNG-to-JPG conversion is **irreversible** — JPG discards pixel data and adds compression artifacts. Keep a PNG backup if you might edit the image again.
Transparent pixels are flattened onto a **white background** because JPG has no alpha channel. If your image has transparency, consider WebP instead.
JPG at **quality 90** typically saves 70–85% file size vs PNG for photos, with no visible quality loss at normal viewing distances.
Screenshots with lots of solid color and text usually compress **better as PNG** than JPG — try both and compare if size matters.

jpgToPng.tipsTitle: Did You Know? JPG to PNG Tips
tips: Converting JPG to PNG doesn't **restore** lost quality — JPG artifacts (block boundaries, ringing around text) remain visible in the PNG.
Use this when you need to **edit a photo** in an app that prefers PNG, or when you want to add transparent regions to an originally opaque JPG.
PNG output is always **lossless** — no quality slider. File size depends solely on image complexity; photos typically grow 3–10× vs the source JPG.
Combine with our **PNG to WebP** tool afterwards to get the editing flexibility of PNG plus the delivery efficiency of WebP.

pngToWebp.tipsTitle: Did You Know? PNG to WebP Tips
tips: PNG → WebP typically shrinks files by **50–80%** with no visible quality loss. Enable **Lossless mode** for guaranteed pixel-perfect output at a modest 20–40% size reduction.
WebP preserves **full transparency** (alpha channel) — a drop-in replacement for PNGs on the web with dramatically better compression.
All evergreen browsers (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari 14+) support WebP. For absolute backwards compatibility, use a `picture` with a PNG fallback.
Google's Core Web Vitals reward smaller images. Converting hero PNGs to WebP often gives an **instant LCP improvement** without any code changes.

webpToPng.tipsTitle: Did You Know? WebP to PNG Tips
tips: **WebP → PNG** is useful when you need to open an image in an older tool (e.g., legacy Photoshop, MS Office, print software) that doesn't support WebP.
PNG output is **lossless** — no further compression artifacts added. If the WebP was originally lossy, the PNG captures that exact visual state.
Expect PNG files to be **2–4× larger** than the original WebP. This is the price of universal compatibility.
Full alpha channel is preserved — if your WebP has transparency, the PNG will too. Useful for separating logos and UI elements.

svgToPng.tipsTitle: Did You Know? SVG to PNG Tips
tips: Use **Scale mode** for retina assets (e.g., 2× or 3×) when your SVG already has correct proportions and you just need a higher-DPI bitmap.
Use **Width only** or **Height only** to resize while preserving aspect ratio — great for generating icons at a specific dimension.
Use **Exact width + height** when you need a specific output like **1200×630 Open Graph images** or **512×512 app icons**, even if the SVG gets stretched.
Our server includes **Noto CJK and emoji fonts** — SVG text containing Chinese, Japanese, Korean characters, or emojis will render correctly.
For the sharpest icons, export your SVG with `viewBox` starting at 0 0 and no outer margins, then rasterize at the exact target size.

faviconGenerator.tipsTitle: Did You Know? Favicon Generator Tips
tips: Upload a **512×512 or larger square PNG** for the best results — all smaller sizes are downscaled cleanly, but upscaling from a small source looks blurry.
The tool generates **7 files** in one shot: `favicon.ico`, 16×16 and 32×32 PNGs, `apple-touch-icon.png` (180×180), Android 192×192 and 512×512, plus a `site.webmanifest` stub.
Copy the **HTML snippet** we provide into your your `head` — it wires up all 7 files correctly for every platform in one paste.
Edit `site.webmanifest` after extraction to set your app's `name` and `short_name` for Android home screen installs (PWA).
If your source is an SVG, run it through our **SVG to PNG** tool first at 512×512, then feed the PNG here.

whatIs.title: What Is a Sprite Sheet?
whatIs.content: A sprite sheet (also called a spritesheet or texture atlas) is a single image file that contains multiple smaller images — typically animation frames — arranged in a grid. Instead of loading dozens of individual image files, game engines and web browsers load one sprite sheet and display each frame by shifting the visible region. This dramatically reduces HTTP requests, lowers memory overhead, and keeps your animations smooth and efficient.
whatIs.content2: Sprite sheets are a fundamental technique in 2D game development, CSS animation, and motion graphics. Engines like Unity, Godot, Phaser, and PixiJS all natively support sprite sheets. On the web, CSS developers use the background-position property to step through frames, creating lightweight animations without JavaScript or video files.

whatIsFrames.title: What Is Frame Extraction?
whatIsFrames.content: Frame extraction is the process of splitting a GIF animation into its individual frames, each saved as a separate PNG image. This is useful when you need to edit specific frames, re-sequence an animation, or import frames individually into a game engine or video editor.
whatIsFrames.content2: Our tool packages all extracted frames into a single ZIP archive for convenient download. Each frame is named with a zero-padded index (e.g., frame_00.png, frame_01.png) so they sort correctly in any file manager or import dialog.

step2.title: 2. Upload Your GIF

You can also enable automatic background removal, which uses a smart algorithm to detect and remove solid-color backgrounds from each frame.

gamedev.content: Sprite sheets are the standard format for 2D character animations, particle effects, and UI elements in game engines. formats.a: We accept GIF files only (both GIF87a and GIF89a standards). The output is always PNG — either a single PNG sprite sheet or multiple PNGs in a ZIP archive.

maxSize.q: What is the maximum file size?
maxSize.a: The maximum input file size is 20 MB. This applies to both direct file uploads and GIF URLs. Most animated GIFs fall well within this limit.

maxFrames.q: Is there a limit on the number of frames?
maxFrames.a: There is no hard limit on frame count. However, GIFs with hundreds of frames will produce very large sprite sheets. For extremely long animations, consider using the Frames mode to extract individual PNGs instead.

transparency.a: Yes. If your original GIF has transparent regions, they are preserved in the output PNG. If you enable background removal, the detected background color is replaced with transparency.

autoColumns.q: How does the auto column layout work?
autoColumns.a: When you leave the Columns field empty, the tool calculates the number of columns as the ceiling of the square root of the total frame count. This produces the closest-to-square grid layout, which is optimal for texture memory and easy to work with in most game engines.

bgRemoval.q: How does automatic background removal work?
bgRemoval.a: The algorithm samples the RGBA color values of the four corner pixels of each frame. If all four corners are within the tolerance threshold of each other, their average color is used as the background target. A flood-fill starting from all four corners then removes all connected pixels within the tolerance range. If the corners are too different from each other, the frame is left unchanged to avoid removing foreground content.

tolerance.q: What tolerance value should I use?
tolerance.a: The default value of 30 works well for most GIFs with clean, solid-color backgrounds. For GIFs with slight gradients or compression artifacts in the background, try increasing to 50–80. Values above 100 become aggressive and may remove foreground pixels that are similar to the background color.

whatIsFramesToGif.title: What Is PNG Frames to GIF Conversion?
whatIsFramesToGif.content: PNG frames to GIF conversion takes a series of individual PNG images and assembles them into a single animated GIF file. Each PNG becomes one frame of the animation, played in sequence at a specified speed. The process preserves transparency from the original PNG files, so characters or objects with transparent backgrounds animate cleanly without unwanted white borders or background artifacts.
whatIsFramesToGif.content2: This is the reverse of frame extraction — instead of splitting an animation apart, you're building one from scratch. It's the standard workflow for game developers, animators, and designers who create each frame individually and need to preview or export the final animation as a GIF. The tool supports up to 100 individual PNG files per conversion, with configurable frame duration ranging from 10 milliseconds to 10 seconds per frame, giving you precise control over animation timing.
whatIsFramesToGif.content3: When assembling frames, you can choose how to handle PNG files with mismatched dimensions. The tool offers three approaches: centering smaller frames on a transparent canvas sized to the largest frame, filling the background with a solid color, or flagging the mismatch as an error so you can fix it before converting. You can also enable filename-based ordering, which sorts frames by the numeric suffix in filenames (e.g., walk_0.png, walk_1.png, walk_2.png), ensuring your animation plays in the correct sequence regardless of upload order.

whatIsSpritesheetToGif.title: What Is Spritesheet to GIF Conversion?
whatIsSpritesheetToGif.content: Spritesheet to GIF conversion slices a single image containing multiple frames arranged in a grid (a spritesheet) and reassembles them into an animated GIF. You specify the grid layout — either by column/row count or pixel cell dimensions — and the tool extracts each cell as a frame. The tool reads frames left-to-right, top-to-bottom, following the standard spritesheet convention used by most game engines and animation tools.
whatIsSpritesheetToGif.content2: This is particularly useful for previewing spritesheet animations without a game engine, sharing sprite animations on platforms that only support GIF, or converting existing game assets into a format suitable for documentation, social media, or design reviews. You can also select specific row and column ranges to extract only a portion of the spritesheet, which is ideal when a single sheet contains multiple animation sequences — such as walk, run, and idle cycles arranged in different rows.
whatIsSpritesheetToGif.content3: The spritesheet slicing mode supports padding between cells, which accounts for the spacing some tools add between frames during export. You can also enable skip-empty mode to automatically detect and discard fully transparent cells, avoiding blank frames at the end of your animation. Whether your spritesheet was created in Aseprite, Photoshop, TexturePacker, or any other tool, the conversion process works with any standard grid-based layout.

whyConvert.title: Why Convert PNG to GIF?
whyConvert.content: GIF remains one of the most universally supported image formats on the internet. Unlike video files or animated PNGs (APNG), GIF animations play automatically in virtually every browser, email client, messaging app, and social media platform without requiring any plugins or JavaScript. This makes GIF the go-to format when you need a lightweight animation that simply works everywhere.
whyConvert.content2: Converting PNG frames or spritesheets to GIF is especially valuable when you want to share animations outside of their original context. Game developers can preview character animations without launching a game engine. Designers can embed animated UI mockups directly in documentation or Slack messages. Artists can showcase their pixel art on platforms that don't support spritesheet playback. In each case, GIF serves as a universal preview format that anyone can view instantly.
whyConvert.content3: GIF animations are also self-contained — a single file holds every frame, the timing information, and the loop count. There's no need for external players, JavaScript libraries, or CSS animations to make them work. This simplicity makes GIF ideal for README files, wikis, email newsletters, and any context where you need an animation that just plays on its own with zero dependencies.

formatsExplained.title: Understanding PNG vs GIF
formatsExplained.content: PNG and GIF are both raster image formats, but they serve different purposes. PNG supports millions of colors (24-bit or 32-bit with alpha transparency), lossless compression, and a single static frame. It's the preferred format for high-quality images, screenshots, and individual animation frames where color accuracy matters. GIF, on the other hand, is limited to a 256-color palette per frame but supports multiple frames in a single file, making it the classic format for simple animations.
formatsExplained.content2: The 256-color limitation of GIF means that converting from PNG may introduce slight color changes if your source images use a wide color range. For pixel art and illustrations with flat colors, this is rarely noticeable. For photographic or gradient-heavy content, the palette reduction can produce visible banding. The tool handles this conversion automatically, selecting the best 256-color palette for your specific frames.
formatsExplained.content3: Another key difference is transparency handling. PNG supports full alpha transparency with 256 levels of opacity, allowing smooth semi-transparent edges. GIF transparency is binary — each pixel is either fully transparent or fully opaque. This means soft edges or semi-transparent overlays in your PNG frames will be converted to hard edges in the GIF output. For best results with transparent GIF animations, use PNG source frames that already have clean, hard-edged transparency.

documentation.title: Technical Documentation

prototyping.title: Design Prototyping
prototyping.content: Quickly assemble UI mockup frames into animated walkthroughs to test animation timing and transitions before committing to a full implementation in code. This approach is faster than building interactive prototypes for early-stage feedback, and the resulting GIF can be shared via email or embedded in presentation slides.

differentSizes.q: What happens if my frames have different sizes?

gridVsCell.q: What's the difference between Grid and Cell slicing mode?

Cell mode works the other way — you provide the exact pixel width and height of each frame, and the tool calculates how many columns and rows fit. Use Grid mode when you know your sheet is organized as, say, 8 columns by 4 rows. Use Cell mode when you know each frame is exactly 64×64 pixels but aren't sure about the grid layout.

whatIs.title: Why Pack PNG Frames into a Sprite Atlas?
whatIs.content: A sprite atlas is the output of packing many individual PNG assets — exported frames, icon sets, tile variants — into a single texture that an engine can sample from. The PNG to Spritesheet workflow is fundamentally a packing problem: you already have a curated set of source files (perhaps a walk cycle exported from Aseprite, or a UI icon pack from a designer), and you need to flatten them into one atlas that your runtime can load in a single texture upload. This tool is built around that authoring step rather than around any conversion from animated formats.
whatIs.content2: For game projects the pay-off is very concrete. Shipping 200 loose PNG files means 200 filesystem reads (or 200 HTTP fetches on web builds), 200 texture uploads, and a draw batch that breaks every time the renderer switches between them. Pack those same assets into one atlas and the runtime issues a single texture bind — Phaser 3, PixiJS, Unity, and Godot can then draw every sprite that lives on the atlas within the same batched draw call. On mobile and WebGL targets, where texture bandwidth and request overhead are the usual bottlenecks, this is often the single largest win you can make in a 2D renderer.
whatIs.content3: Beyond runtime performance, atlases fit cleanly into asset pipelines. Instead of tracking hundreds of individual files through version control, an atlas gives you a single PNG plus a TexturePacker JSON — two artifacts that can be regenerated from source in a build step, checked by CI, and dropped into the engine as a pair. Indie teams and tool authors use this pattern to keep their repo tidy, reduce import churn in engines like Unity and Godot, and bake final atlases as part of a release pipeline.

layouts.title: Grid, Strip, or Bin-Packed: Which Layout?
layouts.content: Unlike tools that force a single layout, the PNG to Spritesheet builder exposes four distinct packing strategies so you can match the output to whatever your engine expects. Grid packing arranges your frames into a rectangular lattice and works well when every input PNG shares the same footprint — classic Aseprite animation exports, character walk cycles, or Godot SpriteFrames sequences all fit this shape. You can pin a specific column count, or leave it empty so the packer reaches for a near-square ceil(sqrt(N)) arrangement that keeps the final texture compact.
layouts.content2: Horizontal and vertical strip packers lay everything on a single axis. Developers reach for strips when they need to drive a fragment shader flipbook that interpolates along U or V, when an engine's animation component expects linearly indexed frames, or when a CSS sprite animation needs to translate a single offset per frame. Strips also produce the most deterministic frame addressing: once you know the cell size, frame N always lives at N × cell on one axis and zero on the other — useful when you are computing UVs inside build scripts or shader code.
layouts.content3: The packed mode runs a bin-packing algorithm over frames of varying sizes and produces an irregular atlas with no wasted whitespace — the layout you want when your input set mixes 16×16 icons with 96×48 buttons, or when a tilemap includes both single tiles and 2×2 decoration clusters. Because frame rectangles are no longer predictable, packed output always ships with a TexturePacker-format JSON that maps filenames to atlas coordinates so engines like Phaser 3 (load.atlas) and PixiJS (Assets.load) can look up each frame by its original name.

formats.title: Engine-Ready Atlas Metadata
formats.content: Every run produces a PNG, and — when metadata is enabled — a companion JSON file describing where each source frame lives on the sheet, all wrapped in a single ZIP. The JSON follows the TexturePacker JSON Array schema, which the rest of the 2D ecosystem has quietly converged on over the past decade. Each entry records the original filename, the frame rectangle on the atlas, the source dimensions of the pre-packed image, and a trim rect for sprites that have been cropped during packing. Tool integrators can rely on this schema staying stable across runs, which matters when the output is being fed into a CI job or an asset-baking step.
formats.content2: Phaser 3 consumes this JSON directly through scene.load.atlas(key, png, json), after which any frame can be referenced by its original filename in animation definitions. PixiJS expects the same schema via its Spritesheet / Assets.load path — drop in the ZIP contents and every frame becomes a Texture keyed by name. For Unity pipelines, the free TexturePacker Importer slices the PNG back into sub-sprites inside the editor so your prefabs and AnimationClips can reference them individually; Godot users can lean on community importer plugins that materialise the JSON into AtlasTexture resources or SpriteFrames for AnimatedSprite2D nodes.
formats.content3: If your engine can infer frame positions from cell dimensions alone — a pure grid in Godot SpriteFrames, for example — you can turn metadata off and collect a lone PNG. Packed mode always includes JSON because the irregular rectangles can't be reconstructed from parameters. The separate power-of-2 toggle pads the final canvas up to 256/512/1024/2048 so it matches GPU sampling alignment requirements on older mobile chipsets and certain texture compression formats; for WebGL 1 contexts that still enforce POT textures for repeat-wrapped samplers, this is the easiest way to stay compatible without touching engine-side settings.

howTo.title: How to Assemble a Sprite Atlas

step1.title: 1. Upload Your Frame Set
step1.content: Drop a curated batch of PNG frames onto the uploader, or pick them from disk — up to 100 files per job at 5 MB each and 60 MB in total. Whether they came from an Aseprite export sequence, a Photoshop layer comp, a Krita animation, or a folder produced by a build script, the files show up as a draggable thumbnail grid. Each thumbnail carries its index badge so you can confirm the order that will be baked into the atlas.

step2.title: 2. Choose Your Packing Layout
step2.content: Open Layout & Options and commit to a packing strategy. Grid is the go-to when every frame shares a bounding box; horizontal and vertical strips give you linear frame addressing for shader-driven or CSS flipbooks; packed unlocks bin-packing for heterogeneous sets like UI atlases and tile variant packs. Switching to packed automatically enables TexturePacker JSON output, since engines cannot infer irregular frame rectangles from parameters alone.

step3.title: 3. Fine-Tune Cell Behavior, Padding, and Ordering
step3.content: For grid and strip layouts, pick a cell mode — auto-max sizes every cell to the largest frame's bounding box (handy when exports drift by a pixel or two), auto-uniform asserts that every frame is the same size and fails fast if not, and fixed locks an exact cell size with fit_mode choosing between scale-fit, scale-fill, or rejection for oversized inputs. Use align to control how smaller frames sit inside oversized cells, add pixel padding to prevent bilinear bleed between neighbours, and flip power-of-2 on if your target GPU or compression format expects POT textures. Turn on filename ordering when your exporter numbers frames with a _N suffix and you want that order enforced regardless of upload sequence.

step4.title: 4. Export the Atlas
step4.content: Hit Convert and the server builds the atlas. You receive either a standalone PNG, or a ZIP bundling the PNG with its TexturePacker JSON when metadata is on. The preview renders the finished sheet inline so you can spot alignment mistakes before committing it to a repo or uploading it to your engine. Download to save the result, or reset the workspace to build the next atlas in your batch.

layouts.title: Four Packing Strategies
layouts.content: Grid for uniform animation exports, horizontal and vertical strips for linear flipbooks and shader-driven sampling, and bin-packed for heterogeneous atlases. Each strategy is tuned to a different runtime consumption pattern, so you can match the output to how your Phaser 3, PixiJS, Unity, or Godot project actually samples the atlas at runtime.

cellModes.title: Cell Sizing for Pipeline Control
cellModes.content: Auto-max adapts to whichever frame is biggest, which is the forgiving choice for exports that drift by a pixel. Auto-uniform turns an assumption into a guarantee — if two frames disagree on size, the job fails loudly so you catch the mismatch in CI instead of in-game. Fixed mode pins an exact cell size with a fit_mode fallback so older asset sets can be normalised into a new atlas dimension.

metadata.title: TexturePacker JSON Output
metadata.content: Optional JSON Array metadata is produced alongside the PNG and packaged in a ZIP. The schema is natively understood by Phaser 3's load.atlas, PixiJS's Assets loader, and — via community importers — Unity and Godot. Because the format is stable and widely supported, the same ZIP can be dropped into different engines without rewriting any glue code.

powerOf2.title: Power-of-2 Texture Padding
powerOf2.content: A single switch rounds the atlas canvas up to 256, 512, 1024, or 2048 px. POT textures are still expected by some compression formats (PVRTC on older iOS, certain WebGL 1 repeat-wrap samplers) and remain the safest default for mipmap-heavy pipelines. Padding pixels respect the configured background color or stay transparent.

reorder.title: Drag-to-Reorder Workflow
reorder.content: The upload grid is a draggable surface: grab a thumbnail and drop it into the right slot to fix frame order without renaming anything on disk. Pair it with filename ordering when your exporter emits walk_0.png, walk_1.png, walk_2.png and you want that numeric suffix to win automatically, which is useful when a build script is appending frames in an unpredictable order.

alignPadding.title: Alignment and Cell Padding
alignPadding.content: When frames are smaller than their cells, align controls whether they sit centered or pinned to the top-left — the latter is what Godot's tilemap and many Unity Sprite Editors expect. Cell padding inserts a transparent buffer between neighbours so bilinear filtering cannot sample across cell boundaries, which stops the hairline seams that show up on scaled sprites in shader-heavy scenes.

privacy.title: Privacy First
privacy.content: Uploads live in memory only long enough to build the atlas, then get discarded. There is no account, no cookie-based tracking of your asset contents, and no server-side archival — which matters when the frames you're packing belong to an unannounced project or a client deliverable under NDA.

gameSprites.title: Indie Game Sprite Pipelines
gameSprites.content: Feed a folder of Aseprite-exported frames — a full character's walk, run, and attack sheets — directly into the packer and ship the resulting atlas to Phaser 3, PixiJS, Unity, or Godot. Combine grid packing with auto-max cells for tidy per-action atlases, or switch to bin-packed when you want to batch an entire character set across mixed frame sizes. Wire the tool into a build script so every art update regenerates the atlas without manual drag-and-drop work.

uiAtlas.title: UI and HUD Texture Atlases
uiAtlas.content: Icon packs, button states, cursor variants, and portrait thumbnails rarely share a consistent size, which makes them a textbook case for bin-packing. Upload the entire UI folder, select packed layout, and the output JSON exposes every element by its filename so PixiJS, Phaser 3, or a custom WebGL UI layer can look frames up by name instead of by hand-authored UV coordinates.

animationAssembly.title: Assembling Engine Exports into Atlases
animationAssembly.content: Aseprite, Krita, and Photoshop all happily export timelines as numbered PNG sequences — and then leave you to stitch them together. This tool is the stitching step: drop the sequence, enable filename ordering so walk_0.png through walk_23.png line up, and produce a grid atlas with a TexturePacker JSON ready for AnimatedSprite2D in Godot or Phaser 3's createFromAseprite-equivalent workflow.

tilesets.title: Tileset and Asset-Baking Pipelines
tilesets.content: Pack ground tiles, wall variants, and prop decorations into a uniform-grid atlas aligned to a 16×16 or 32×32 cell, or drive the packer from a CI/CD job that regenerates the atlas every time raw art changes. Fixed cell mode plus top-left alignment produces sheets that snap cleanly into Godot's TileSet resource and Unity's Tile Palette, making this a natural fit for asset-baking stages of a release pipeline.

whatIsSheet.q: How is a sprite atlas different from just a folder of PNGs?
whatIsSheet.a: Functionally, an atlas lets your engine perform a single texture bind for every sprite on the sheet, whereas loose PNGs force a separate bind (and often a separate draw call) per file. For a typical 2D scene that is the difference between one batched draw and dozens of unbatched ones. The companion JSON gives you the lookup table so you still reference individual frames by their original filename in code.

whichLayout.q: Grid, strip, or packed — how do I pick?
whichLayout.a: Default to grid when your input PNGs share a bounding box (character animations, tile variants). Pick horizontal or vertical strip when you need predictable linear addressing for a shader flipbook or a CSS animation. Reach for packed when the frame set mixes sizes — UI icon collections, prop sheets, or any folder that a designer curated without regard for uniformity. Packed layouts always bundle JSON metadata because the rectangles are irregular.

maxFiles.q: How many PNG frames can I pack in one atlas?
maxFiles.a: Up to 100 files per job, with a 5 MB per-file cap and a 60 MB combined cap. That limit exists to keep server processing fast; for most indie atlases — a full character's animation set, a tile pack, a UI component library — it's comfortably above what you would ever put on a single sheet in practice.

metadata.q: Does the JSON work with Phaser 3's load.atlas out of the box?
metadata.a: Yes. The output is TexturePacker JSON Array, which is exactly what scene.load.atlas(key, pngUrl, jsonUrl) expects. After loading, each frame is addressable by its original PNG filename, so phrases like scene.add.sprite(x, y, 'character', 'walk_0.png') just work. PixiJS's Spritesheet parser and Assets.load accept the same ZIP contents without modification.

engines.q: Which engines have native support for the output?
engines.a: Phaser 3 and PixiJS load the PNG+JSON pair natively. For Unity, the free TexturePacker Importer reads the JSON and slices the PNG into editor sub-sprites so you can drag individual frames into prefabs. Godot users can install a community TexturePacker Importer plugin that produces AtlasTexture resources or SpriteFrames for AnimatedSprite2D. Any other engine that can sample from a PNG will at worst need a thin JSON parser on top.

powerOf2.q: When does power-of-2 padding actually matter?
powerOf2.a: Modern desktop and recent mobile GPUs no longer require POT textures for basic sampling. However, some GPU compression formats (PVRTC on older iOS), WebGL 1 contexts using GL_REPEAT on a non-POT texture, and certain mipmap-generation paths still need power-of-2 dimensions. If you are targeting those environments, or your engine's import settings prefer POT, turn it on — otherwise the smaller, tight-fit atlas is usually the right choice.

transparency.q: Can I reorder frames after uploading them?
transparency.a: Yes — the thumbnail grid is draggable, so you can swap positions by grabbing a frame and dropping it into a new slot. This is useful when your file picker hands files back in a different order than your authoring tool used. If the source names encode order as a numeric suffix (walk_0.png, walk_1.png, ...), turn on filename ordering and the packer will enforce that order regardless of upload sequence.

privacy.q: Are my PNGs stored or shared?
privacy.a: No. The server holds your PNG frames only long enough to build the atlas, then discards them once the response is sent. There is no account system, no logging of asset contents, and no third-party sharing — relevant if the artwork you are packing belongs to an unreleased project, a client under NDA, or a closed-source pipeline.

whatIs.title: What Is PNG Trim?
whatIs.content: PNG trim is the process of automatically cropping away the transparent pixels around the edges of a PNG image, shrinking the canvas down to the smallest rectangle that still contains all the opaque (or partially opaque) content. Most design and animation tools — Photoshop, Aseprite, Spine, game engine exporters — produce PNG files with large transparent margins, because the export canvas is typically sized to the artboard or the largest frame in a sequence rather than to the actual sprite.
whatIs.content2: That extra transparent padding is invisible to the eye but very real on disk and in memory. It inflates file sizes, wastes VRAM when the sprite is uploaded as a texture, and confuses bounding-box logic in game engines that rely on sprite dimensions for collision, layout, or hit-testing. A trim pass fixes all of these issues in one step by recalculating each sprite's true bounding box and exporting only the meaningful pixel region.
whatIs.content3: This tool runs that trim pass for you in your browser. Upload a single PNG or a whole batch, set an optional alpha threshold and padding value, and download either a single trimmed PNG or a ZIP of trimmed files. The original visual content and transparency are preserved exactly — the tool only removes empty margin pixels.

whyTrim.title: Why Trim Transparent Edges?
whyTrim.content: The most immediate benefit of trimming is smaller file sizes. Transparent padding still takes up pixel rows and columns in the PNG, and while compression handles large runs of transparency efficiently, eliminating them outright produces noticeably smaller files — often 30-70% reductions for sprites exported onto oversized canvases. Smaller files load faster, fit more comfortably into mobile memory budgets, and transfer faster over the network.
whyTrim.content2: The second benefit is accurate bounding boxes. Game engines typically use a sprite's PNG dimensions as its default hitbox, pivot origin reference, and render extent. A sprite that's 128×128 pixels but contains a 40×60 character in the middle of an otherwise transparent canvas produces collision and alignment bugs because the engine sees a 128×128 hitbox. Trimming the PNG to its true content means your engine sees the real sprite size, and everything downstream — collisions, UI layouts, click targets, tooltip anchoring — works correctly without manual offsets.
whyTrim.content3: Trimming also produces cleaner sprite atlases when you later pack sprites into a spritesheet. Bin-packing algorithms can only minimize the final atlas size when each input is already tight. If every sprite carries a 20-pixel transparent border, the packer wastes those pixels in every cell. Trim first, pack second, and you'll get a dramatically smaller and more efficient texture atlas.

howItWorks.title: How the Alpha Threshold Works
howItWorks.content: The trim algorithm scans each PNG pixel by pixel to find the tightest bounding box that encloses all non-empty pixels. The question of what counts as empty is controlled by the alpha threshold parameter. Alpha values range from 0 (fully transparent) to 255 (fully opaque). With a threshold of 0, only fully transparent pixels (alpha = 0) are treated as empty and trimmed; any pixel with alpha ≥ 1 is considered content and preserved.
howItWorks.content2: Increasing the threshold makes the algorithm more aggressive. A threshold of 10 treats pixels with alpha 0-10 as empty — useful when your PNG has faint anti-aliasing ghosts or near-invisible noise pixels at the edges that you want stripped. Thresholds of 30-50 are appropriate when sprites have soft fading shadows or glow edges that you consider decorative rather than meaningful content. Going higher than 100 tends to trim visible semi-transparent effects, so use cautiously.
howItWorks.content3: After finding the bounding box, the tool optionally adds a configurable padding — a transparent border of N pixels around the trimmed content. Padding is useful when you plan to pack the trimmed sprite into a spritesheet or apply bilinear filtering in-engine, because it prevents texture bleeding at the sprite's edge. A padding of 1-2 pixels is usually sufficient for most rendering pipelines.

gameSprites.title: Preparing Game Sprites for Packing
gameSprites.content: Export your character and prop sprites from Aseprite, Photoshop, or Spine with their full artboards intact, then run this tool to trim every file to its true content size. Trimmed sprites pack into dramatically smaller atlases — bin-packers only minimize space when each input is already tight, so removing transparent borders first can cut your final atlas size in half or more.

uiIcons.title: Cleaning UI Icon Exports
uiIcons.content: Design apps often export icons at fixed canvas sizes (256×256, 512×512) regardless of the actual icon dimensions. Run your icon exports through the trim tool to get crisp, correctly-sized assets where the icon fills the PNG. Bounding-box-driven UI systems will then size and position icons correctly without needing manual padding offsets in code.

animationFrames.title: Batch Trimming Animation Frames
animationFrames.content: Drop in a whole folder of animation frames exported from your animation tool — a walk cycle, an explosion sequence, a spell effect — and get a ZIP of all frames trimmed in one pass. This is the necessary first step before assembling frames into a spritesheet with the packed layout, because packed layouts rely on tight bounding boxes for efficient packing.

atlasReduction.title: Reducing Sprite Atlas Size
atlasReduction.content: If your existing sprite atlases are bigger than they should be, trimming the individual source PNGs before re-packing often reveals significant savings. Projects that trim aggressively before atlasing routinely see 40-60% smaller atlas textures, which translates directly to faster asset loads and lower VRAM usage — especially valuable for mobile and web builds.

threshold.q: What alpha threshold should I use?
threshold.a: Start with the default of 0, which only trims fully transparent pixels and is safe for every clean PNG. If your source files have faint anti-aliasing ghosts, near-invisible noise pixels, or soft fade effects at the edges that you want removed, try a threshold between 10 and 30. Anything above 100 will start trimming visible semi-transparent content, so raise it carefully and preview the result.

padding.a: Not usually. Leave padding at 0 for most workflows to get the tightest possible bounding box. Add 1-2 pixels of padding if you plan to pack the trimmed PNG into a spritesheet, or if your game engine uses bilinear texture filtering and you want to avoid edge bleeding artifacts. More than 2 pixels of padding defeats much of the space-saving benefit of trimming.

singleVsBatch.q: What's the difference between single and batch output?
singleVsBatch.a: If you upload a single PNG, you get back a single trimmed PNG that you can preview and download. If you upload two or more PNGs, you get back a ZIP containing every trimmed file with the original filenames preserved. There's no configuration to switch between the two — it's determined automatically by the number of files you upload.

compatibility.q: Does the trimmed PNG work in game engines and design tools?
compatibility.a: Yes. The output is a standard PNG with alpha channel preserved, readable by any engine, design app, or browser that handles PNG files — which is essentially all of them. Trimming only crops the canvas; it doesn't change the PNG's color profile, bit depth, or compression format.

maxFiles.q: How many PNGs can I trim at once?
maxFiles.a: Up to 100 PNG files per batch, with each file up to 5 MB and a combined total of 60 MB. These limits are generous for practically any animation sequence or icon set you would batch-trim in one go.

transparency.q: Does trimming affect transparency or image quality?
transparency.a: No. The trim operation is purely a crop — it removes empty rows and columns of pixels from the PNG's margins without re-sampling, re-compressing, or altering any content pixel. Semi-transparent pixels, soft edges, and partial alpha values are preserved byte-for-byte in the output.

privacy.q: Are my files stored on the server?
privacy.a: No. Your PNG uploads are processed in memory and immediately discarded after the trimmed result is returned. No account is required, no logs are kept of your file contents, and no cookies track your uploads. The trim happens, the result is returned, and every trace of your upload is gone.

whatIs.title: What Is Spritesheet Splitting?
whatIs.content: Spritesheet splitting (also called atlas extraction or spritesheet slicing) is the reverse of spritesheet generation: instead of merging individual PNG frames into a single texture atlas, it slices an existing spritesheet back into its constituent parts. The tool reads a grid-based PNG, extracts each cell as a separate frame, and optionally generates a TexturePacker-compatible JSON or CSS metadata file that maps frame names to their pixel coordinates on the original sheet.
whatIs.content2: Spritesheet splitting is a common step in game development pipelines when you receive pre-built atlas assets — purchased from an asset store, exported from a game engine, or provided by a designer — and need to work with individual frames. Instead of manually cropping every cell in Photoshop or Aseprite, a splitter reads the grid dimensions and produces a clean, numbered set of PNG files in seconds. The same operation can produce atlas metadata that lets you load the original spritesheet directly in Phaser 3, PixiJS, Unity, or Godot without re-assembling anything.
whatIs.content3: This tool is the companion to our PNG to Spritesheet generator. Use the packer when you have loose frames and need to combine them; use the splitter when you have an atlas and need to extract or document its contents. Both tools share the same Easy PNG to Sprites API, which powers either direction of the spritesheet authoring workflow in a single service.

outputs.title: Three Output Modes: Frames, Metadata, or Both
outputs.content: Frames mode extracts every cell from the spritesheet as an individual PNG file, packages them in a ZIP archive with zero-padded sequential filenames (frame_0.png, frame_1.png, ...), and returns that archive for download. This is the mode to reach for when you need the source images themselves — to edit specific frames, re-time an animation, or re-pack the frames in a different layout using the PNG to Spritesheet tool.
outputs.content2: Metadata-only mode skips pixel extraction entirely. It reads the grid coordinates of each cell and produces a machine-readable atlas description — JSON Array, JSON Hash, or CSS Sprites — describing exactly where each frame sits on the spritesheet. This mode is ideal when you already have the spritesheet PNG in your project and just need the coordinate file to load it in an engine. No image data is extracted, which means faster processing and a smaller download.
outputs.content3: Both mode produces a single ZIP containing all extracted frame PNGs plus the atlas metadata file. This is the most complete output: it gives you the spritesheet data in an engine-ready format alongside the individual frames you might need for further editing. Use this mode when you're encountering an unknown spritesheet for the first time and want a full picture of its structure before deciding how to integrate it.

metadataFormats.title: Choosing a Metadata Format
metadataFormats.content: JSON Array is the default format and the one with the broadest engine support. It follows the TexturePacker JSON Array schema — the de facto standard in the 2D game ecosystem — where each frame is described by a filename, a frame rectangle, and source size fields. Phaser 3 loads this format natively with scene.load.atlas(), and PixiJS accepts it through Assets.load(). Every extracted frame is addressable by its generated filename (frame_0.png, frame_1.png, ...) so engine code stays clean without hardcoding pixel coordinates.
metadataFormats.content2: JSON Hash uses the same TexturePacker schema but structures the frames field as an object keyed by filename rather than an array. Some engines and community importers default to hash format — for example, certain Unity TexturePacker Importer configurations. If your loading code or engine plugin explicitly expects a hash-keyed frames object, use this option. Otherwise JSON Array is the safer default, as it has wider first-party support across Phaser 3, PixiJS, and most community tools.
metadataFormats.content3: CSS Sprites generates a stylesheet where each frame becomes a CSS class with background-position, width, and height values targeting its coordinates on the source spritesheet. Drop the spritesheet PNG and the generated CSS file into a web project, reference the sheet as a background-image, and use the class names to display individual sprites. This is the classic technique for CSS sprite animations and icon sheets, and is ideal for web UI projects that don't use a JavaScript game engine.

step1.title: 1. Upload Your Spritesheet
step1.content: Drag and drop a single spritesheet PNG onto the upload area, or click to open the file picker. The file can be up to 20 MB. A thumbnail preview loads immediately so you can confirm you have the right file before configuring the split parameters.

step2.title: 2. Set the Slicing Mode and Grid
step2.content: Choose Grid mode if you know the number of columns and rows in your spritesheet — for example, a 4-column by 3-row sheet. Choose Cell mode if you know the pixel dimensions of each frame — for example, 64×64 pixels per cell. If the spritesheet has outer whitespace around the grid, use Trim Margins to crop it before slicing. If there are pixel gaps between cells (gutters), set Cell Padding to match.

step3.title: 3. Configure Output and Filters
step3.content: Choose an output mode: Frames extracts individual PNGs into a ZIP, Metadata generates an atlas description file without extracting pixels, and Both gives you everything in one ZIP. When metadata is selected, pick the format: JSON Array for Phaser 3 and PixiJS, JSON Hash for some Unity importer plugins, and CSS Sprites for web projects. Use Column Range and Row Range to target a specific animation sequence within the sheet, and Frame Count to cap the total number of frames extracted.

step4.title: 4. Download the Result
step4.content: Click Split to process the spritesheet. The server slices the PNG, applies your filters, and returns the result — typically under a second for most sheets. Download the ZIP, JSON, or CSS file and drop it into your project. Click "Split Another" to clear the workspace and start a fresh split with a new file.

gridAndCell.title: Grid and Cell Slicing Modes
gridAndCell.content: Two ways to define the slice grid: specify column and row counts when you know the layout structure, or specify the pixel width and height of each cell when you know the frame size. Grid mode divides image dimensions by the column and row counts to determine cell size. Cell mode divides image dimensions by the cell size to determine the grid layout. Both modes produce the same output for a given spritesheet — the choice depends on what information you have.

allOutputModes.title: All Three Output Modes
allOutputModes.content: Extract individual PNG frames, generate atlas metadata without touching pixels, or produce both in a single request. Match the output to your workflow: frames-only for editing and re-packing, metadata-only for engine integration when you already have the PNG, and both for a complete picture of an unfamiliar atlas. The metadata-only mode is significantly faster because it skips all pixel-level image processing.

metadataFormats.title: Three Atlas Metadata Formats
metadataFormats.content: JSON Array (TexturePacker standard, natively supported by Phaser 3 and PixiJS), JSON Hash (hash-keyed variant for importers that expect object-structured frames), and CSS Sprites (ready-to-use stylesheet for web background-position animations). All three formats are generated from the same slicing pass — pick the one your target runtime or engine expects and download it in the same request.

rangeSelection.title: Partial Extraction with Range Filters
rangeSelection.content: Use column and row range filters (e.g., columns "2-5", rows "1-3") to extract only specific cells from a larger spritesheet. This is essential for spritesheets that pack multiple animation sequences into a single texture — walk cycles, attack sequences, and idle animations in different row bands. Target exactly the sequence you need without splitting the whole atlas, and combine with Frame Count to cap the output to a precise number of frames.

trimAndPadding.title: Trim Margins and Cell Padding
trimAndPadding.content: Strip outer borders from the spritesheet before slicing with four independent trim inputs (top, right, bottom, left), and account for inter-cell gutters with Cell Padding. Many spritesheets exported from TexturePacker, Aseprite, Photoshop, or game engines include outer whitespace and inter-frame gaps that would otherwise misalign the slice grid. Setting these parameters correctly is the most common fix when frames appear shifted or incorrectly cut.

skipEmpty.title: Skip Empty Frame Detection
skipEmpty.content: When enabled, the tool scans each extracted cell for pixel content and discards fully transparent ones. This handles the common case where a spritesheet's last row is incomplete — for example, 14 frames arranged in a 4-column grid produces a final row with 2 blank cells. Skip Empty removes those blank frames automatically so your output contains only meaningful images with no placeholder files at the end of the sequence.

singleFile.title: Up to 20 MB Spritesheet Input
singleFile.content: Accepts a single PNG file up to 20 MB. This comfortably covers production-grade spritesheets, including high-resolution 4096×4096 and 8192×8192 atlases commonly used for game characters and tilesets. The file is processed server-side, so your browser's available memory does not affect the split.

privacy.title: Privacy First
privacy.content: Your spritesheet is processed in memory on the server and discarded immediately after the response is returned. No account required, no persistent storage, no logging of file contents or pixel data. Relevant when the artwork you are splitting belongs to an unannounced project, a client asset under NDA, or a closed-source pipeline.

engineIntegration.title: Generating Atlas JSON for Existing Spritesheets
engineIntegration.content: If you have a spritesheet PNG without its companion JSON file — downloaded from an asset store, sent by a designer, or exported without metadata — use metadata-only mode to regenerate the atlas description. Choose JSON Array for Phaser 3 or PixiJS, JSON Hash for certain Unity importer plugins, or CSS Sprites for web animation. The output is a ready-to-use atlas file that pairs directly with your existing PNG, so you can load the spritesheet into your engine immediately without re-packing or re-exporting.

frameExtraction.title: Extracting Frames for Re-editing
frameExtraction.content: When a game asset needs to be updated but you only have the final spritesheet — not the individual source files — frame extraction gives you back the original cells as individual PNGs. Extract the frames, edit the specific ones you need in Aseprite, Photoshop, or any pixel editor, then re-pack the updated set with the PNG to Spritesheet tool. This is a common recovery workflow in game jam projects, asset-store updates, and team handoffs where the original source files are unavailable.

partialExtraction.title: Pulling One Animation from a Multi-Sequence Sheet
partialExtraction.content: Production spritesheets often pack multiple animation sequences into a single texture — a character's walk cycle in rows 0–1, attack in rows 2–3, and idle in rows 4–5. Use row and column range filters to target exactly the sequence you need. The result is a clean, isolated frame set or sub-spritesheet for that specific animation, without forcing you to extract and sift through the entire atlas. Combine with Frame Count to handle sequences whose last row is incomplete.

cssAnimations.title: Building CSS Sprite Animations
cssAnimations.content: Upload a spritesheet, set metadata format to CSS Sprites, and download a stylesheet where every frame is a ready-made CSS class carrying background-position, width, and height. Pair it with the spritesheet PNG in your web project, reference the sheet as a background image on a div, apply the frame classes, and step through them with a CSS keyframe animation using steps(). No JavaScript required — just a background-image and a CSS animation sequence. This technique is widely used for icon sprites, loading indicators, and lightweight character animations on the web.

gridVsCell.q: What's the difference between Grid and Cell mode?
gridVsCell.a: Grid mode asks for the number of columns and rows, then calculates cell size by dividing image dimensions by those counts. Cell mode asks for the pixel width and height of each cell, then calculates how many columns and rows fit. Use Grid mode when you know the layout structure (e.g., "this is a 4×3 grid"). Use Cell mode when you know the frame size (e.g., "each frame is 64×64 pixels"). Both produce identical output for the same spritesheet — the choice depends on what you know about the source asset.

rangeFormat.q: How do I format column and row ranges?
rangeFormat.a: Ranges are 0-indexed. Write a single number to extract one column or row (e.g., "2" extracts only the third column), or a hyphen-separated pair to extract a span (e.g., "1-3" extracts columns 1, 2, and 3). Both column range and row range filter independently — combine them to extract a rectangular region. Leave either field empty to include all columns or all rows. For example, Column Range "0-3" and Row Range "2" extracts a 4-column, 1-row strip from the third row of the sheet.

skipEmpty.q: When should I turn off Skip Empty?
skipEmpty.a: Skip Empty is on by default and handles incomplete last rows cleanly. Turn it off if your animation intentionally includes blank frames — for example, a blink cycle where a transparent frame creates a deliberate pause, or a flash effect that uses an empty cell as a hold frame. With Skip Empty disabled, every cell is extracted regardless of content, giving you a frame count that exactly matches the grid dimensions.

padding.q: My frames look shifted or overlapping — what should I check?
padding.a: The most likely cause is unapplied cell padding or outer margins. If the source spritesheet has pixel gaps between cells (gutters from TexturePacker or Aseprite exports), set Cell Padding to match that gap. If the sheet has outer whitespace around the grid, use Trim Margins to crop it before slicing. A quick check: multiply your expected cell dimensions by the column and row counts, add padding and margins, and compare the total against the actual image dimensions. Any discrepancy points to unconfigured padding or trim values.

metadataFormat.q: Which metadata format should I use?
metadataFormat.a: JSON Array is the safe default: it's natively supported by Phaser 3 (scene.load.atlas) and PixiJS (Assets.load), and accepted by most Unity TexturePacker importer plugins. Use JSON Hash if your specific engine importer or loading library explicitly expects a hash-keyed frames object. Use CSS Sprites if you're building a web project that uses CSS background-position animations without a JavaScript game engine.

outputFormats.q: What file types does the tool return?
outputFormats.a: Frames mode returns a ZIP containing individual PNG files. Metadata-only mode returns a standalone JSON file (for JSON Array or JSON Hash) or a CSS file (for CSS Sprites) — no ZIP wrapper for these. Both mode returns a ZIP containing all frame PNGs plus the metadata file. ZIPs are ready to extract and drop into your project. Standalone JSON and CSS files are ready to place alongside your spritesheet PNG.

maxSize.q: What is the maximum spritesheet size?
maxSize.a: The input spritesheet PNG can be up to 20 MB. There is no hard limit on pixel dimensions, but very large sheets (8192×8192 and above) may take a few extra seconds to process. All processing happens server-side, so your device's available memory or GPU does not affect the split.

privacy.q: Is my spritesheet stored on the server?
privacy.a: No. The uploaded PNG is held in server memory only for the duration of processing and discarded immediately after the response is returned. No file is written to disk, no pixel content is logged, and no account is required. Relevant when the spritesheet contains unreleased artwork, client assets under NDA, or proprietary game content.

whatIs.title: What Is HEIC, and Why Convert to JPG?
whatIs.content: HEIC (High Efficiency Image Container) is the default photo format on iPhone and iPad since iOS 11. It offers roughly 50% smaller files than JPG at the same visual quality, thanks to the underlying HEVC compression. whatIs.title: What Is SVG to PNG Rasterization?
whatIs.content: SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) is an XML-based format that describes images as geometric instructions — paths, shapes, text, and fills — rather than pixels. This lets SVG render at any size without quality loss, perfect for logos, icons, and diagrams.
whatIs.content2: PNG is pixel-based (raster). Rasterization converts the SVG's instructions into actual pixels at a specific resolution. Once rasterized, the image is fixed at that size — upscaling a PNG loses quality, unlike SVG.
whatIs.content3: You rasterize when you need a specific PNG output for a platform that doesn't accept SVG: Open Graph social previews, favicons, app store icons, Slack emoji, print assets, or Word/PowerPoint embeds.

sizing.title: Three Ways to Size Your Output
sizing.content: **Scale multiplier** — multiplies the SVG's native viewBox. Use this when your SVG already has correct proportions and you just need a retina (2×) or print-ready (4×) bitmap.
sizing.content2: **Width only** or **Height only** — set one dimension, the other is computed from the SVG's aspect ratio. Great for generating icons at a specific width without worrying about height math.
sizing.content3: **Exact width × height** — forces the output to exactly these dimensions. If your aspect ratio differs from the SVG's, the image will be stretched. Useful for fixed-size requirements like Open Graph (1200×630).

whatIs.title: What Is a Favicon, and Why Do You Need a Full Pack?
whatIs.content: A favicon is the small icon that represents your website in browser tabs, bookmarks, mobile home screens, and search results. In 2025, supporting every device properly requires not just one `favicon.ico` but a coordinated set of images at specific sizes — the classic ICO, high-DPI PNGs for modern browsers, an Apple Touch Icon for iOS home screens, and Android Chrome icons for Progressive Web Apps.
whatIs.content2: Getting this right manually is tedious: you need to export your logo at 7 different sizes, generate a multi-resolution ICO, produce a web manifest, and remember the exact HTML link tags for each device. Skip or misconfigure one, and you end up with a blurry 16×16 scaled from the wrong master, a generic placeholder on iOS, or a broken PWA install prompt.
whatIs.content3: This tool generates the complete pack from one source image in seconds — all 7 files at correct sizes, plus a ready-to-paste HTML snippet that wires everything up for every platform in the right order.
